conclusion.title: Conclusion:
conclusion.lead: This is my honest project conclusion. Not polished to just "look good", but as it really was: lots of detours, lots of corrections, and in the end a system that is far more robust than at the start.
conclusion.leadSecondary: I deliberately did not want a standard recap full of empty buzzwords. I wanted to show the path you usually do not see in commit histories and logs: decisions under pressure, technical fractures, and the learnings that came out of them.

acts.title: The Start Was Harder Than Expected
paragraphs: [[React was a real construction site at the beginning]]. I had too many dependencies between components, state drift between the web app and extension, and multiple flows overwriting each other.
This was especially visible in chat: streaming, editing, regenerate, image upload, history, and auth all had to work correctly at the same time. At first it often worked "somehow", but not reliably.

The turning point was to separate responsibilities consistently: clearer component boundaries, reproducible user flows, and fewer quick fixes directly in the UI. Only then did the project start feeling like a real product instead of a demo with many loose pieces.

acts.title: Database Reality: PostgreSQL to SQLite
paragraphs: Originally, PostgreSQL was my planned default path. In practice, that was exactly where friction kept returning: local setup, migration workflows, consistent environments across machines, and unnecessary complexity for the current product stage.
The move to [[SQLite with WAL]] was therefore not a fallback, but a deliberate product decision. I wanted a data foundation that runs locally, fast, stable, and without side battles.
The result was clear: less time lost to infrastructure stress, more time for real features, bug fixes, and consistency. For this project phase, that switch was exactly right.

acts.title: First Time with Three.js and 3D Assets
paragraphs: [[Three.js was completely new to me]]. I had to learn FBX import, material handling, camera logic, performance, and rendering errors at the same time while the rest of the app kept moving in parallel.

At the beginning it was pure trial and error: textures did not load, scenes were too dark, animations felt artificial or restless. But that exact phase was important because it taught me which camera and motion decisions actually feel cinematic and which ones are just loud.
In the end, this produced a visual language that is not interchangeable: more atmosphere, more staging, and still technically controlled enough to keep the page stable.

acts.title: The Real Leap: Quality in the Details
paragraphs: The biggest progress did not come from one new feature, but from the "invisible" construction sites: clean intent routing, clarification flow without overtriggering, consistent response language, robust streaming behavior, and clear error fallbacks.
That is where it is decided whether an AI product only impresses or actually works in day-to-day usage. If routing, language, context, and UI do not align, even the best model cannot save it.
My core learning from this act: [[not just build features, but stabilize behavior]]. That is what creates trust in the product.

acts.title: Keeping Two Worlds in Sync: Web App and Extension
paragraphs: One point I underestimated before: keeping [[the same logic stable across two different interfaces]]. In the web app and extension, small differences instantly feel like two separate products when language, popup behavior, input states, or error texts are not perfectly aligned.

That is exactly why I [[standardized many things]]: identical clarification rules, consistent markdown/code rendering paths, clean fallbacks, and the same behavior during streaming interruptions. It was not spectacular, but it massively improved perceived quality.
The learning from this act was clear: when a product lives across multiple surfaces, [[consistency is not optional, it is a core feature]].

acts.title: Release Pressure, Setbacks, and Clean Decisions
paragraphs: Toward the end, it became less about "one more feature" and more about [[prioritization]]. I had to consciously decide more often what not to build so that what remained would actually stay stable. Especially [[under time pressure]], this is harder than it sounds.

There were setbacks too: things that looked good short-term created side effects later and had to be removed again. Rolling back was frustrating at first, but necessary to [[keep a clear technical line]].
Maybe the most important effect of this phase: I now think more in [[maintainability and behavior over time]], not only in "works right now".

reflection.title: What This Project Changed in Me
reflection.intro: When I summarize the entire path today, the biggest difference is not only visible in the result, but especially in [[the way I approach problems]].
reflection.quickTitle: If I break it down to four points:
quick: [[Quality emerges in edge cases and transitions.]]
[[Debugging is a core process, not an emergency mode.]]

chapters.title: 1) From Screen Thinking to System Thinking
paragraphs: Today I think much more in systems instead of isolated screens. A good screen matters, but [[without stable data paths, clear routing, and clean state management]] it remains surface only. That insight was probably the biggest step of the whole project.
When I look back at the beginning now, I see less the individual features and more the shift in mindset: from "I build something that somehow runs" to [["I design something that behaves reliably"]].

chapters.title: 2) Courage to Correct Course
paragraphs: At the same time, I learned to correct technical decisions with confidence. The PostgreSQL-to-SQLite switch is a good example: do not stick to a plan just because it sounded "right" at the beginning, but [[choose what is truly sensible for the current product state]].

In hindsight, this exact mix was decisive: frontend sensitivity, backend discipline, and readiness to rethink architecture when reality demands it. Earlier I would have defended some decisions for too long, now [[I correct earlier and more cleanly]].

chapters.title: 3) Quality Emerges Between the Lines
paragraphs: I realized that product quality often emerges in transitions: in timeouts, error texts, reconnect logic, language consistency, and exactly when users do not follow the happy path. That is where it is decided whether [[trust grows or breaks]].

And personally, Three.js was the part that created the most growth for me: not because everything worked immediately, but because real problems taught me to [[combine visual quality with technical stability]].

chapters.title: 4) System Beats Motivation
paragraphs: Professionally, I learned that debugging is not an "emergency mode" but a normal development process. Good logs, reproducible steps, and small targeted fixes moved this project faster than big risky rebuilds.

Personally, I learned that a project of this size is not carried by motivation alone, but by [[systematic execution]]: setting priorities, documenting decisions, and finishing things before opening the next block.

reflection.keyline: Progress in practice rarely looks spectacular. It is built through many clean decisions that only together feel like a [[big leap]].

finale: My conclusion in one sentence: [[Wieland AI did not become strong through one big breakthrough, but through many hard and concrete decisions under real pressure]].
That is exactly why this conclusion does not feel like an ending to me, but like the point where experiments turned into a clear direction.
